title: Accelerated TMS in Autism Spectrum Disorder with Depression
subtitle: Hopeful news in for young people who are often left out!
body_html:
One of the more important questions in the world of transcranial magnetic stimulation has been the treatment of individuals who have more than just depression. I'm a child psychiatrist, so a lot of the individuals who come to see me have autistic spectrum disorders—this is true for adults Psychiatrist also. Still, as child psychiatrists, we have more experience making this diagnosis.

Differences have been noted in the cortical excitability—how easy it is to make neurons to fire—between autistic and non-autistic individuals. However, the exact mechanisms of this and how much this mattered were not clear:

[a] systematic review showed that short-interval intracortical inhibition was likely to be reduced in individuals with ASD compared with controls with mild to moderate effect size, whereas there was no difference in motor-evoked potentials (with single-pulse TMS stimulation—ED) amplitude between the two groups.1

I've had years of not knowing what to do and to what degree TMS might be helpful. This has been the subject of many phone calls between myself and colleagues like Eleanor Cole, Ph.D., who knows a hell of a lot more about this than I do!

We have data suggesting hyperexcitability2, so should they be stimulated more or less? For general audiences, I'm going to skip the basic science and get to the point: We have a paper published that demonstrates accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation (aTMS) is an effective treatment for depression in individuals with autism.

Blank et. al3. Used a relatively low-dose accelerated protocol, three stimulations a day times 10 days, in 10 individuals who were “transitional age”—that is, in their early 20s. This may sound like a small sample, and it is, but keep in mind FDA-clearance for SAINT was obtained in under 40 participants!

It worked for depression…(the HDRS-17 is a depression rating scale):

This is the first trial for aTMS in individuals with autism—so they carefully looked at other endpoints in an open-label trial. Let’s start with what I didn’t expect to see…It helped subjects sleep:

Sleep

For PSQI Score, … p = 0.018, EF = 0.799 and demonstrated a large treatment effect …significant improvement in sleep ratings at Week 4: t(19) = 3.19, p = 0.023, estimated change = 4.38…

It was also beneficial in anxiety symptoms (on the GAD-7, a standard anxiety measure I use in Osmind all the time.):

The last graph on the right is each subject displayed separately. Two people go no benefit at all, and others did very well. There are some non-responders in brain stimulation trials across the board, so this is in keeping with my expectations.

It's exciting to see researchers evaluating treatments for individuals traditionally ruled out of clinical trials. This is better for equity across human suffering and families who need to know what to do for their kids.

Thanks for reading!

1

Masuda, F., Nakajima, S., Miyazaki, T. et al. Motor cortex excitability and inhibitory imbalance in autism spectrum disorder assessed with transcranial magnetic stimulation: a systematic review. Transl Psychiatry 9, 110 (2019). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-019-0444-3

2

Takarae, Y., & Sweeney, J. (2017). Neural hyperexcitability in autism spectrum disorders. Brain sciences, 7(10), 129.

3

Blank, E., Gilbert, D.L., Wu, S.W. et al. Accelerated Theta Burst Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Refractory Depression in Autism Spectrum Disorder. J Autism Dev Disord (2024). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-024-06244-2
